body:
# Clean local development workspace and lightweight localhost deployment source

## Problem Statement

The RetailMind development workspace and GitHub repository contain accumulated temporary images, browser captures, generated outputs, scratch files, and historical deployment instructions. These make the codebase difficult for the team to navigate and add unnecessary material to deployment downloads. Some output directories also contain authored manuals, original research inputs, scripts, and useful evidence, so deleting entire directories would lose important work.

The intended deployment is a fresh installation on a Windows Store PC, downloaded from GitHub through Git clone. That PC hosts the application and database; existing Cloudflare Tunnel functionality provides online access to the same installation. Automatic deployment to the hosted Hostinger demo is no longer wanted.

## Solution

Clean both the local development workspace and the current GitHub source tree without refactoring application logic. Delete confirmed disposable temporary images and other useless scratch artifacts from disk and Git tracking, organize retained material, prevent generated clutter from returning, and make the existing project documentation a dependable navigation and setup guide.

Preserve Git history and document shallow cloning for deployment downloads. Remove automatic Hostinger deployment while retaining useful automated checks. Document a fresh localhost installation and the existing Cloudflare setup rather than presenting hosted deployment as the primary workflow.

## User Stories

1. As a developer, I want a tidy repository root, so that I can identify application entry points and project resources quickly.
2. As a developer, I want the existing project map to reflect real locations, so that I can navigate the codebase without guessing.
3. As a team member, I want obsolete temporary images deleted locally, so that useless screenshots do not distract from current work.
4. As a developer, I want disposable logs and scratch files removed after checking their uses, so that cleanup does not leave unexplained clutter.
5. As a maintainer, I want artifact classification before deletion, so that fixtures, authored scripts, and important evidence survive.
6. As a maintainer, I want generated artifacts excluded from future commits, so that the repository stays clean.
7. As a developer, I want current local tools, dependencies, and active worktrees preserved, so that cleanup does not interrupt development.
8. As a team member, I want manuals and original research data in documented locations, so that important work remains discoverable.
9. As a reviewer, I want retained evidence references to resolve, so that I can distinguish preserved verification from disposable captures.
10. As an installer, I want a lightweight shallow clone, so that I can download the current deployment source without all historical revisions.
11. As a maintainer, I want Git history preserved, so that existing commits and collaboration references remain usable.
12. As an installer, I want complete fresh localhost instructions, so that I can prepare a new Store PC without relying on the developer's existing machine.
13. As an installer, I want required dependencies and downloads distinguished from optional development tools, so that I install only what each task needs.
14. As an installer, I want explicit empty-database setup instructions, so that I can initialize a fresh Store safely.
15. As a Store operator, I want credentials, uploads, database contents, and Recovery Keys protected during development cleanup, so that operational data is not lost or exposed.
16. As an installer, I want background jobs and private recovery storage covered in setup guidance, so that installation includes the existing operational requirements.
17. As a Super Administrator, I want the existing local Cloudflare setup documented, so that I can enable online access to the Store PC.
18. As a remote Staff Account holder, I want current Workspace permissions preserved through the tunnel, so that repository cleanup does not change application behavior.
19. As a maintainer, I want Hostinger auto-deployment removed, so that pushing source does not upload it to the old hosted target.
20. As a developer, I want useful CI checks retained, so that removing deployment does not remove unrelated verification.
21. As a maintainer, I want obsolete deployment-specific tests adjusted, so that the test suite agrees with the chosen deployment workflow.
22. As an installer, I want required application assets, schema, migrations, and setup files present in a clean checkout, so that a fresh clone remains usable.
23. As a reviewer, I want measured before-and-after file counts and sizes, so that I can assess the cleanup's effect.
24. As a team member, I want incomplete machine-level verification reported explicitly, so that written instructions are not mistaken for a proven Store PC installation.

## Implementation Decisions

- Scope includes local development organization, current tracked repository contents, documentation, ignore rules, and removal of hosted auto-deployment. Application refactoring is separate work.
- GitHub main remains the deployment source. Preserve existing commit history and use a depth-one clone in deployment instructions. Removing current files does not remove their historical versions; do not claim ordinary full clones become equally small.
- Inventory candidate files and their consumers before deletion. Check runtime code, tests, scripts, fixtures, documentation, and relevant tool configuration. Distinguish files read as inputs from screenshot paths that are merely generated outputs.
- The user's latest cleanup decision supersedes the earlier proposal to preserve every disposable artifact in a local archive: confirmed useless temporary images and scratch files are deleted locally as well as removed from tracking. No duplicate trash archive is required.
- Do not blanket-delete output or temporary directories. Preserve or organize authored scripts, manuals, original datasets, reviewed workbooks, notebooks, necessary fixtures, and useful curated verification evidence. Update references when retained material moves; remove stale references to intentionally discarded disposable evidence where appropriate without erasing useful historical findings.
- Prefer existing documentation and archive categories. Avoid a new folder taxonomy or relocating working application modules solely for appearance. Important retained work must remain discoverable; do not silently move unique source material into an ignored location.
- Keep intentionally tracked generated assets required by the application, including its shared stylesheet bundle. Preserve database schemas, migrations, required seed data, product assets, dependency manifests, tests, and required runtime placeholders.
- Review tracked model binaries and runtime assets individually. An ignore pattern or a generated-looking name does not establish that an existing tracked file is disposable.
- Preserve local environment configuration, private recovery material, databases, uploads, installed dependencies, active tool configuration, and worktrees. Follow the existing root working-tree guardrail and preserve concurrent user changes.
- Extend ignore rules for confirmed generated clutter using the current directory layout. Already tracked disposable files must actually leave tracking; ignore rules alone are insufficient.
- Remove the automatic Hostinger deployment workflow and its active setup instructions. Adjust or remove the deployment-only contract and its runner invocation; retain independently useful package/configuration checks and existing Contracts and Playwright workflows.
- Do not change the existing hosted website, remote credentials, or database. Stopping future workflow uploads does not take the hosted site offline. Updating GitHub source requires a later explicit commit/push workflow; publishing this specification does not publish implementation changes.
- Make the main README, documentation index, project map, and deployment checklist consistent with fresh Windows localhost installation and existing Cloudflare access. Label retained hosted-demo material as historical/reference material rather than current deployment instructions.
- Document required local web/database services, supported runtime dependencies, local configuration, fresh empty-database initialization, initial credential replacement, private recovery storage, and existing background-job setup. Explain developer-only test dependencies separately. Derive commands from current source; correct references to absent directories rather than inventing replacements or bundling a runtime redesign.
- Document the existing tunnel provisioning/download route so a fresh clone does not depend on an ignored executable already present on the development PC. Preserve current authorization and Workspace boundaries: the Super Administrator stays local-only, while tunnel sessions retain the existing permitted Workspace behavior.
- No schema, API, role-capability, or application-module interface changes are intended. Existing local-deployment and tunnel decisions apply; older read-only tunnel requirements must not override the later full-Workspace-parity decision.

## Testing Decisions

- Primary acceptance boundary: the resulting repository checkout, its documented fresh-install workflow, and retained existing verification commands. Test observable outcomes rather than asserting an arbitrary folder arrangement or duplicating ignore patterns in new tests.
- Run the existing aggregate stylesheet/view/smoke/tunnel checks and deterministic contracts. These are existing repository seams; no new testing framework is needed.
- Adjust the hosted-deployment-only contract and its suite integration to reflect removal of auto-deployment. Run affected independently useful packaging/configuration checks and check retained workflow definitions for obsolete dependencies on the removed workflow.
- Validate references for moved or removed material, including links in the README, documentation indexes, project map, operational guides, research notes, and affected tests/scripts. Confirm retained fixtures remain readable and browser-output directories can still be created by their existing producers.
- Check that disposable files are absent from both local candidate locations and the tracked tree, that new representative generated artifacts are ignored, and that important retained assets remain available.
- Compare before-and-after tracked artifact counts and checkout sizes. Report the actual reduction separately from historical Git storage; do not invent a numeric size target.
- Verify a clean shallow checkout of the resulting revision contains required application, setup, schema, dependency, and documentation inputs. Do not rely on ignored dependencies, local environment files, model caches, or tunnel binaries from the developer's existing installation.
- Where feasible, follow fresh-install instructions against a disposable empty local database, then verify login and the current initial setup flow. Never import the fresh schema into the developer's or an operating Store's database.
- Machine-level Windows service startup, Cloudflare token/domain provisioning, hardware, and full fresh-PC operation require their actual environment. Report any such checks not performed; do not count a documentation review as a successful installation or change live services merely to validate cleanup.
- These seams synthesize the existing repository checks and agreed no-refactor scope. No additional interview or new test architecture is required for this specification.

## Out of Scope

- Application logic refactoring, module redesign, route moves, UI redesign, or new features.
- Git history rewriting, force pushes, branch pruning, or worktree removal.
- Installing on an actual Store PC, importing a real database, starting/stopping services, provisioning Cloudflare accounts/domains, or changing tunnel permissions as part of writing this spec.
- Upgrading or migrating an existing Store; the documented target is a fresh installation.
- Deleting important manuals, original research inputs, necessary fixtures, operational data, credentials, or Recovery Keys.
- Decommissioning the hosted website or deleting hosted databases and account secrets.
- Broad deletion of historical documentation or evidence solely because it is old.
- Running the cleanup, committing it, or pushing implementation changes during this specification-only task.

## Further Notes

The user explicitly paused cleanup and requested synthesis and publication first. No cleanup, local artifact deletion, deployment change, or database mutation has been performed in this session; only this planning document has been written.

Read-only inspection found approximately 1,871 tracked temporary-directory files, 173 primary-output files, 10 secondary-output files, 151 design-review files, four Word documents, and a root research ZIP. These are starting inventory counts, not a safe-delete list; remeasure when implementation begins.

Important findings include original research CSVs/workbooks and a notebook among outputs, a PDF manual among generated-looking material, intentionally tracked product images and stylesheet output, and a tracked model binary needing classification. Existing documentation references a missing development-work index and an absent legacy forecasting directory. These must be resolved through inspection rather than wholesale deletion or unverified setup instructions.

Local main matched the cached remote reference during initial inspection, but live remote freshness and the current hosted revision were not verified. The future implementation should report actual local changes, verification results, remaining limitations, and any later commit/push status accurately.
title: Clean local workspace and GitHub source for fresh localhost deployment

# Scheduled Backups, Recovery-Key Prompts, and Keyring Management

## Problem Statement

Store operators must remember to create every Database Backup manually. When they forget, the only copy of Store history is the live database and its uploads. Previous backup packages also collect with no rule for which copy should remain, recovery-key copies are easy to forget, and a Recovery Key imported from another server cannot be listed, promoted, exported, or removed.

Restoring a package made on a different database structure fails during review with an incompatible-structure message, even when the package's data is valid. The destination's own backup history may also carry a stale structure that makes history queries fail. Operators are left with a dead end instead of a clear upgrade path.

## Solution

A Scheduled Backup runs automatically every week without an operator present, contains the database and referenced uploads, is written to a configurable Backup Destination outside the web document root, and replaces the previous Scheduled Backup only after the new package is verified. The schedule, destination, and next run are visible to the Super Administrator, and a missed run is caught up once when the Store PC returns.

After every backup, the system recommends saving the Recovery Key separately and keeps recommending it until the responsible administrator acknowledges that specific key. The Recovery Key manager becomes a Backup Keyring: importing a key saves it immediately without replacing the Primary Recovery Key, and the administrator can keep both, promote the imported key to primary while archiving the old primary, export any key, or delete a key after an explicit password-confirmed warning.

Restore accepts packages from known older database structures by upgrading their rows to the current structure, preserves the destination's own migration ledger, and rejects unknown or newer structures with a clear list of what the destination does not understand.

## User Stories

1. As a Super Administrator, I want Scheduled Backups to run every week without anyone pressing a button, so that a forgotten manual backup cannot leave the Store without a recent copy.
2. As a Super Administrator, I want to choose the weekday and local time of the weekly schedule, so that backups suit the Store's closing hours.
3. As a Super Administrator, I want the schedule to default to Sunday at 11:00 PM, so that a working schedule exists before I configure anything.
4. As a Super Administrator, I want to see the next scheduled run, so that I know when the next automatic copy should appear.
5. As a Super Administrator, I want a missed Scheduled Backup to catch up once when the Store PC is next available, so that a power interruption does not leave a long gap.
6. As a Super Administrator, I want catch-up to run at most once regardless of how many weeks were missed, so that the system does not create redundant packages.
7. As a Super Administrator, I want to choose the Backup Destination, with a sensible default, so that automatic copies live on the disk I intend.
8. As a Super Administrator, I want the Backup Destination to be rejected when it sits inside the application or web document root, so that packages cannot be downloaded by URL.
9. As a Super Administrator, I want the previous Scheduled Backup removed after the new one is verified, so that weekly disk use stays bounded.
10. As a Super Administrator, I want the previous Scheduled Backup kept when the new attempt fails, so that a failed run never leaves zero automatic copies.
11. As a Super Administrator, I want manual backups and restore safety copies unaffected by Scheduled Backup retention, so that recovery evidence is never deleted unexpectedly.
12. As a Super Administrator, I want replaced Scheduled Backups marked as removed in backup history rather than silently disappearing, so that the retention action is auditable.
13. As a Super Administrator, I want backup history to show whether a row is a manual, scheduled, or restore package and whether its file still exists, so that I can tell evidence from a stale link.
14. As a Super Administrator, I want a failed Scheduled Backup to raise an attention item and, when enabled, a Store Email Alert, so that failure is not discovered only by chance.
15. As a Super Administrator, I want a Scheduled Backup to skip when another backup or recovery is active, so that it cannot collide with a manual operation.
16. As a Super Administrator, I want a skipped Scheduled Backup recorded and retried on the next run, so that a busy system does not lose the week's copy.
17. As a Super Administrator, I want the weekly run to work from the Windows scheduler without a signed-in browser, so that automation does not depend on someone keeping a tab open.
18. As a Super Administrator, I want an in-app catch-up path when the Windows task did not run, so that a disabled or missed task still recovers.
19. As a Super Administrator, I want each Scheduled Backup to include the database and referenced uploads, so that restoring it returns a complete Store.
20. As a Super Administrator, I want the new package authenticated and validated before the previous one is removed, so that retention cannot delete a good copy for a damaged one.
21. As an Administrator, I want a prompt recommending that I download the Recovery Key after a backup, so that I am reminded before I forget.
22. As an Administrator, I want the prompt on my next sign-in with a persistent banner until handled, so that an unattended Scheduled Backup still reaches a person.
23. As an Administrator, I want the prompt at most once per session, so that it does not interrupt every page.
24. As an Administrator, I want downloading the Recovery Key to require my current login password, so that possession of an open session alone is not enough.
25. As an Administrator, I want the system to acknowledge the specific key only after a successful download, so that a dismissed prompt is not mistaken for a saved key.
26. As an Administrator, I want the banner to disappear for me after I acknowledge the key, while another administrator who has not saved it still sees the recommendation, so that responsibility is personal.
27. As a Super Administrator, I want the same recommendation and acknowledgement behavior as an Administrator, so that either role can act.
28. As an Administrator, I want importing a Recovery Key from another server to save it immediately, so that the package can be opened without another step.
29. As an Administrator, I want importing to keep the destination's Primary Recovery Key by default, so that existing packages are not stranded.
30. As an Administrator, I want the option to use the imported key for new backups, so that a migrated installation can adopt its source key deliberately.
31. As an Administrator, I want the old primary key archived rather than deleted when I promote an imported key, so that packages made with it remain recoverable.
32. As an Administrator, I want to see every key in the Backup Keyring with its fingerprint, kind, and date, so that I can identify what I hold.
33. As an Administrator, I want to export any key in the Backup Keyring, not only the primary one, so that I can move a source key back to another installation.
34. As an Administrator, I want deleting a key to require an explicit warning and my current login password, so that I cannot erase the only way to open old packages by accident.
35. As an Administrator, I want the primary key protected from deletion until another key is promoted, so that new backups always have a usable encryption key.
36. As a Super Administrator, I want key import, export, promotion, and deletion recorded in the activity log, so that key custody changes are attributable.
37. As an Administrator, I want to restore a package made on a known older database structure, so that an older Store Migration copy is not rejected.
38. As an Administrator, I want an unknown or newer database structure rejected with the missing migration names, so that I know whether to upgrade the destination or use a newer RetailMind.
39. As an Administrator, I want the destination's migration ledger preserved during restore, so that restoring an old snapshot does not roll the installation backward.
40. As an Administrator, I want the destination's backup history structure repaired by the normal migration path, so that a partially upgraded installation stops failing history and restore review.
41. As an Administrator, I want review to tell me whether a package is current, upgradable, or unsupported before I confirm replacement, so that I am not surprised after choosing accounts.
42. As a Super Administrator, I want only my role to change the schedule, destination, and retention behavior, so that an ordinary Administrator cannot redirect Store evidence.
43. As an Administrator, I want to keep creating manual backups, so that I can capture a copy before a risky change.
44. As a Super Administrator, I want the Backup Keyring and compatibility reports to avoid secrets in logs, URLs, and filenames, so that recovery evidence is not leaked by metadata.
45. As a Super Administrator, I want Scheduled Backup history to record which key fingerprint encrypted the package, so that the download recommendation matches the actual package.

## Implementation Decisions

### Scheduling and execution

- Add a **Scheduled Backup** service that decides whether a run is due, delegates package creation to the existing `DatabaseBackupService`, applies retention after verification, and records outcome. It must be callable from both a CLI entry point and an authenticated in-app path.
- Schedule state lives in platform-level settings owned by the Super Administrator: weekday (0-6), local time (HH:MM), destination path, and last successful run. Default is Sunday 23:00 in the application timezone.
- The Windows scheduled-task installer gains one RetailMind weekly-backup task. The installer remains idempotent. Because settings can change after installation, the task runs frequently enough to notice the configured time (hourly) and the service decides if the week's run is due; this avoids rewriting the Windows task on every settings save.
- Catch-up runs once when the newest successful Scheduled Backup is more than seven days old. Multiple missed weeks collapse into one run. Catch-up is throttled so it cannot run on every page load.
- A run skips when recovery is paused, another backup holds the active-operation slot, or an ML job blocks capture. The skip is recorded, and the run may be retried by the next scheduled tick or catch-up check.
- Manual backups, restore safety copies, and restore evidence are outside retention. Retention targets only packages recorded as Scheduled Backups.
- Retention runs only after the new package passes its existing decode and structural verification. It removes the previous scheduled artifact, marks its history row as removed, and never removes the current package.
- Destination validation requires an absolute path outside both the application root and the web document root, writable access, and the existing free-space threshold. Invalid configuration fails closed with an actionable message.
- Automatic packages use a stable name that includes the local timestamp and keep a history row. The download endpoint resolves only artifacts recorded for the requester's installation and authorized role.
- Failure produces an attention item and, when Store Email Alerts are enabled, one email. Repeated failures do not send a message per retry within the same day.

### Recovery-key recommendation

- Every completed backup history row records the encryption key fingerprint that the package header already carries.
- A per-account acknowledgement record ties a user to a key fingerprint and acknowledgement time. The recommendation appears when the newest completed backup's fingerprint has no acknowledgement for that account.
- The recommendation is a one-time-per-session modal plus a persistent banner. The banner disappears for an account once that account downloads the matching key.
- Acknowledgement is recorded only after the download stream completes successfully. Cancelled or failed downloads do not acknowledge.
- The existing current-password authorization and local-request checks remain in force. The recommendation links to the existing Recovery Key area rather than creating a second download path.

### Backup Keyring

- Extend the key store with list, promote, archive, delete, and export-by-fingerprint operations alongside the existing current-key generation, lookup, and additive import.
- Import remains additive and immediate. Importing the same key again is idempotent.
- Promotion writes the imported key as the Primary Recovery Key and archives the previous primary under its fingerprint, so old packages remain decryptable. Archiving is not deletion.
- Deleting an imported key is allowed only after explicit password-confirmed warning that its packages become unrecoverable. Deleting the Primary Recovery Key is blocked while it is primary.
- The key manager lists fingerprint, kind (primary or imported), and dates. Any listed key can be exported after current-password verification.
- Key import, export, promotion, archive, and deletion are activity-logged with fingerprints and filenames only; key material never appears in logs, URLs, or audit metadata.

### Database-structure compatibility

- The package manifest gains the set of applied migration keys and the encryption key fingerprint. Compatibility is decided from migration history plus the schema fingerprint, not from the fingerprint alone.
- Capture excludes `schema_migrations` rows while still recording the applied keys in the manifest. Restore preserves the destination's migration ledger instead of overwriting it from the package.
- Add a registered upgrade-adapter registry. Each known older migration range maps to a transformation that produces rows for the current destination structure. Adapters run on package rows before destination-table replacement.
- Review classifies packages as current, upgradable, or unsupported. Upgradable packages continue through the existing identity reconciliation, safety-copy, replacement, and reopening flow. Unsupported packages stop before destructive work and name the missing migrations or the newer format.
- Unknown newer structures are never guessed at. They are rejected with an actionable message.
- Replace the ad-hoc backup-schema bootstrap with the migration runner so that a partially upgraded installation repairs its backup history table through the normal path. Existing installations receive an idempotent migration adding the new history columns.
- Preserve the existing rule that destination security state remains authoritative. An older package may change Store records but may not weaken destination accounts, roles, or session policy.

### Settings and permissions

- Schedule, destination, and retention behavior are platform-governance settings. Only the Super Administrator changes them.
- Administrators retain manual backup creation, restore review, recovery-key actions, and read-only visibility of schedule status and backup history.
- Setting changes are activity-logged.

## Testing Decisions

Good tests assert observable behavior through stable seams: package creation, key files and HTTP responses, restore outcomes, CLI exit behavior, and rendered page affordances. Tests must not reach into private methods or assert exact internal file layouts beyond the documented contract.

Preferred seams, reusing existing ones:

1. **Backup creation seam** — `DatabaseBackupService` and the CLI backup entry point. Test package contents, history rows, retention, skip behavior, and failure preservation without a browser.
2. **Scheduled-run seam** — the new scheduled service with an injected clock and temporary destination. Test due, not-due, catch-up-once, busy-skip, and failed-run behavior.
3. **Key-management seam** — the key store plus the recovery-key HTTP endpoint. Test additive import, promotion with archive, blocked primary deletion, explicit delete, export by fingerprint, password requirement, and acknowledgement-on-complete-download.
4. **Restore-compatibility seam** — `SqlBackupFormat` and `DatabaseRestoreService` with generated packages from known older structures. Test current, upgradable, unknown-older, and newer rejection; verify the destination migration ledger survives.
5. **Browser seam** — authenticated Super Administrator and Administrator pages. Test schedule settings visibility, key manager actions, prompt modal and banner, and the acknowledgement disappearing per account.

Prior art to follow:

- Package-format and cross-install key tests in the existing store-package test suite.
- Backup workflow and safety-copy integration tests using the MySQL test database.
- Restore browser tests that create a package, download it, and re-upload it.
- Recovery-tools browser tests that render backup tabs and key forms.
- Route-contract tests for authorization and local-request behavior.

Verification should run the existing style, view, and smoke checks plus the backup-specific unit, integration, and browser suites.

## Out of Scope

- Cloud storage, offsite replication, or third-party backup services.
- Hosted-cron deployment examples; this iteration covers the Store PC Windows scheduler plus in-app catch-up.
- Configurable retention counts other than one; keeping the newest Scheduled Backup is fixed for now.
- Backing up application code, configuration, or the private recovery store itself.
- Automatic restore or automatic Store Reopening.
- Key escrow, password-based key derivation, or recovery without holding a key.
- Legacy `RMSTORE1` passphrase packages.
- Redesigning the backup screen beyond what the new controls require.
- Multi-store or multi-tenant backup scheduling.

## Further Notes

- The reported incompatible-structure failure was assumed to occur during restore review for a package from an older backup on the same installation. If it also occurs during backup creation, the destination-schema repair work in this spec must be expanded first.
- `docs/BACKUP_RECOVERY.md` and `docs/STORE_PACKAGE_FORMAT.md` still describe legacy passphrase packages that the current code rejects. Documentation should be corrected alongside implementation.
- The dashboard description of a backup as a plain SQL Store copy is stale and should be corrected.
- Windows permissions are best effort: the code requests private modes, but the host filesystem may not reflect them. The Backup Destination must still be outside the web root.
- The application timezone is Asia/Manila in the current environment; schedule evaluation uses the application timezone, not the operating system's.
- The current private recovery store already sits outside the web root; the Backup Destination is a separate, user-chosen retention location for Scheduled Backups.
- Related decisions: ADR-0021 (portable schemas without replaying source DDL), ADR-0023 (password-authorized restoration), ADR-0024 (administrator self-authorized restore), and ADR-0028 (scheduled weekly backups and managed key custody).
title: Scheduled weekly backups, recovery-key prompts, and keyring management

# One-paste Remote Access setup on the Store PC

## Problem Statement

RetailMind runs on one Windows Store PC with XAMPP already installed, and the application source and database are already in place. Enabling Remote Access still requires the operator to locate the tunnel installer, open an elevated PowerShell, paste the Cloudflare tunnel token, and know which script to run. The Super Administrator already holds the token in the Remote Access card, but has no single path from that card to a running, boot-persistent tunnel. A second machine is not part of the deployment: this Store PC is the sole live host.

The owner has no domain yet. A permanent named Cloudflare Tunnel cannot be created without a Cloudflare zone, so an interim Quick Tunnel is required until a domain is purchased.

## Solution

Extend the existing Remote Access card in Platform Settings with a **Generate Store PC setup block** action. The generated block is a self-contained PowerShell snippet that the Super Administrator pastes once into an elevated PowerShell on the same Store PC. The block runs pre-flight checks, provisions the portable `cloudflared` binary, persists the tunnel token, registers the RetailMind tunnel Windows Service with automatic startup and crash recovery, starts it, and prints the resulting state.

When a permanent token is saved, the block provisions the named tunnel. When no token is saved, the block provisions a Quick Tunnel instead and clearly labels it as interim, URL-changing, and without a Cloudflare Access gate. Saving a token later and regenerating the block upgrades the same PC without source changes.

The card also shows a short Cloudflare dashboard checklist and a matching removal block. Generation is local-only, capability-gated, CSRF-protected, and audit-logged; the raw token is never rendered until the Super Administrator explicitly generates a block.

## User Stories

1. As the Super Administrator, I want to open one card and get one setup block, so that I do not need to locate scripts or reconstruct commands.
2. As the Super Administrator, I want to copy the block into an elevated PowerShell once, so that Remote Access is running without editing files.
3. As the Super Administrator, I want the block to install `cloudflared` itself, so that the Store PC does not depend on a pre-installed binary.
4. As the Super Administrator, I want the tunnel registered as a Windows Service, so that Remote Access returns after a reboot or power outage without a Windows login.
5. As the Super Administrator, I want the service to restart after a crash, so that a transient failure does not require a store visit.
6. As the Super Administrator, I want the block to fail fast when the local application is not reachable, so that I do not publish a tunnel to a dead local server.
7. As the Super Administrator, I want the block to remove the legacy Quick Tunnel scheduled task when a permanent service is installed, so that two tunnels never fight over the same route.
8. As the Super Administrator, I want to re-run the same block safely, so that I can repair a broken service or apply a changed token.
9. As the Super Administrator, I want an interim Quick Tunnel block while no domain exists, so that I can use remote monitoring now.
10. As the Super Administrator, I want the interim block labeled with its limits, so that I do not mistake a changing URL for a stable address.
11. As the Super Administrator, I want a checklist for the Cloudflare dashboard steps, so that tunnel creation, hostname, and Access policy are not guessed.
12. As the Super Administrator, I want a removal block in the same card, so that I can cleanly disable Remote Access or move to another PC.
13. As the Super Administrator, I want the token hidden until I generate a block, so that it is not exposed on a passively viewed screen.
14. As the Super Administrator, I want every generation recorded, so that token exposure has an accountable owner.
15. As the Store owner, I want the setup to use the existing token and hostname fields, so that buying a domain later requires no rework.
16. As the Super Administrator, I want the block to embed the resolved application root and local port, so that I do not edit deployment paths by hand.
17. As the Super Administrator, I want a clear message when I paste the block into a non-elevated shell, so that I know to reopen PowerShell as Administrator.
18. As the Super Administrator, I want the same service name in Quick and permanent modes, so that switching modes does not leave two services behind.
19. As a Cashier, I want the setup change to leave local checkout untouched, so that remote access work cannot alter sales behavior.
20. As the Store owner, I want remote access to remain unavailable when the PC, local services, or internet is down, so that the setup does not imply cloud hosting.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Surface:** Extend the existing Remote Access section of Platform Settings. Do not add a navigation entry or a new page.
- **Authorization and locality:** Reuse the existing platform-governance capability and local-request requirement. Generation is a CSRF-protected POST action. The raw token is read only at generation time and is masked in the default view.
- **Block builder:** Put block construction in a small, pure builder module that returns the PowerShell text from explicit inputs: application root, local port, token, hostname, and mode. Keeping it pure lets tests assert the generated artifact without executing PowerShell.
- **Reuse the existing installer:** The generated block is a thin wrapper that runs pre-flight checks, then invokes the existing tunnel installer and removal script. Do not fork a second service installer. Extend the existing installer with a Quick Tunnel mode rather than adding a parallel script.
- **Pre-flight:** Require an elevated PowerShell, 64-bit Windows, internet access, and a reachable local application origin on the configured port. Report, rather than silently ignore, an existing service or legacy scheduled task.
- **Persistence:** The Windows Service uses automatic startup and `sc.exe` failure restart actions. The token is persisted through the existing tunnel configuration path so the application status card stays accurate.
- **Idempotency:** A re-run stops, deletes, and recreates the service, matching current installer behavior. Re-running is the supported repair path.
- **Mode selection:** A saved token plus hostname yields a permanent named-tunnel block. No saved token yields an interim Quick Tunnel block. Both modes share the same service name and local origin check.
- **Interim labeling:** The Quick Tunnel block and the card state must state that the URL changes on restart and that Cloudflare Access is not in front of it. RetailMind sign-in and the application read-only boundary remain in force.
- **Cloudflare checklist:** The card lists creating a tunnel, adding a public hostname (requires an owned domain), creating the owner-only Access policy, and copying the tunnel token. No Cloudflare API automation and no domain purchase are included.
- **App root:** Because the Super Administrator views the card on the same Store PC, the block embeds the resolved application root and configured local port; the operator does not edit paths.
- **Removal:** The card exposes a removal block that stops and deletes the service and removes the legacy scheduled task. It does not delete the application, database, or backups.
- **Audit:** Each generation writes one activity record naming the actor and the selected mode. The record excludes the token and the generated block.
- **No scope creep:** The setup block does not install XAMPP, Apache, PHP, or MySQL, does not import the database, and does not copy source files. Those remain manual preparation steps completed before setup.
- **Seam:** The primary test seam is the rendered Remote Access card and the generated block text, exercised through the existing PHP contract-test pattern. PowerShell service behavior is verified by a manual Windows acceptance checklist because CI cannot install Windows services.

## Testing Decisions

- **What makes a good test:** Assert observable artifacts and state transitions, not private helper calls or script internals. The generated block is the artifact; its mode, embedded root, port, service commands, and token placement are externally visible behavior.
- **Card contract tests:** Assert that the token is masked by default, that generation requires local request, platform governance, and CSRF, and that a successful generation renders the block and an audit record without exposing the token elsewhere.
- **Builder tests:** Cover permanent mode, Quick mode, blank token, hostname present without a token, and path or port values that need quoting. Assert that the token appears only inside the generated command and never in the audit payload.
- **Mode tests:** Assert that saving a token switches subsequent generation to the permanent block and that clearing it returns to the Quick Tunnel block.
- **Prior art:** Reuse the existing Cloudflare tunnel orchestrator contract, global header tunnel pill contract, and mobile QR modal contract patterns, which load the card and assert user-visible behavior and authorization boundaries.
- **Manual Windows acceptance:** Paste the block into a non-elevated shell and confirm a clear exit message; paste into an elevated shell and confirm the service reaches RUNNING. Reboot and confirm Remote Access returns without a login. Re-run and confirm repair. Run the removal block and confirm the service and legacy task disappear. Verify local checkout and printing during an internet outage.
- **Mode acceptance:** With no token, confirm an interim Quick Tunnel URL appears and is labeled. After saving a token and hostname, regenerate and confirm the named tunnel starts and the card reports the permanent hostname.

## Out of Scope

- Installing or configuring XAMPP, Apache, PHP, or MySQL.
- Copying application source or importing the database.
- Purchasing a domain or automating Cloudflare account, tunnel, or Access creation.
- Self-updating setup blocks or background version checks.
- Changing remote read-only enforcement, which remains governed by ADR-0019.
- A second live Store PC, multi-store ingress, or cloud database replication.

## Further Notes

This spec supersedes the Quick Tunnel exclusion in the owner remote monitoring specification only for the interim period before an owner-controlled domain exists, as recorded in ADR-0027. The permanent path remains the named tunnel with Cloudflare Access described in ADR-0019. The setup block is a deployment convenience, not a new runtime dependency: removing it leaves the application, database, and local checkout unaffected.
title: One-paste Remote Access setup on the Store PC

## Problem Statement

As a retail store owner and system stakeholder, I need absolute assurance that every promised function and feature of the RetailMind store management platform is thoroughly tested, structurally robust, and free of hidden bugs or data anomalies. I want to verify that core retail promises—including cashier transactions, GCash payment processing, batch inventory calculations, supplier receiving, automated replenishment, administrative oversight, and disaster recovery—are implemented well enough for production operation. Additionally, I need high-yield UI/UX improvements identified and integrated so that retail cashiers and managers can operate with maximum transaction velocity and minimal cognitive friction.

## Solution

Implement an exhaustive, vertical role-sliced audit and automated verification harness covering all 116 application views and backing domain services. The solution establishes four objective quality gates (financial/ledger integrity, role boundaries, offline fault tolerance, and audit traceability) and audits each feature through a tri-fold inspection engine (static markup/CSS checks, backend contract tests with transactional rollbacks, and browser-based user journey tests). High-yield ergonomics enhancements—such as cashier keyboard hotkeys, barcode auto-focus, compact table density, non-jumping pagination, and double-submit prevention on financial operations—are systematically captured and applied across all four workspace roles.

## User Stories

1. As a Cashier, I want the barcode search field to auto-focus immediately upon opening the POS or completing a sale, so that I can scan customer products without reaching for the mouse.
2. As a Cashier, I want keyboard shortcuts (Enter to initiate payment, Esc to dismiss dialogues), so that I can ring up high-volume sales rapidly during peak hours.
3. As a Cashier, I want the payment submission button to disable immediately upon click, so that I do not accidentally record duplicate sales or double-charge a customer.
4. As a Cashier, I want held cart recovery to preserve all scanned items and discount promotions accurately, so that I can assist another waiting customer without losing the customer's items.
5. As a Cashier, I want the GCash payment view to validate reference number formatting before submission, so that typos and invalid transaction references are caught before finalizing the sale.
6. As a Cashier, I want the shift opening and closing view to provide a denomination counter for Philippine peso bills and coins, so that I can reconcile register cash drawer counts quickly and accurately.
7. As a Cashier, I want a clear discrepancy warning when closing a shift if the physical count does not match expected register sales, so that cash variances are investigated immediately.
8. As a Cashier, I want Cash Refund requests to link directly to the original sale receipt, so that items cannot be refunded for more than their original transaction amount.
9. As a Cashier, I want to submit stock issue reports for broken or spoiled store items directly from my terminal, so that inventory managers are alerted to shelf losses immediately.
10. As an Inventory Manager, I want real-time stock status filters with color-coded badges for expired, expiring soon, low stock, and out of stock, so that I can prioritize shelf restocking and removal without manual guesswork.
11. As an Inventory Manager, I want batch inventory deductions to follow FIFO and track batch expiration dates, so that older stock is sold before fresher stock.
12. As an Inventory Manager, I want physical inventory count reconciliation sheets that calculate surplus and deficit variances automatically, so that periodic stocktaking updates the ledger transparently.
13. As an Inventory Manager, I want supplier receiving workflows to capture purchase orders, batch numbers, and expiration dates in a high-density grid, so that bulk deliveries are received efficiently.
14. As an Inventory Manager, I want the automated replenishment queue to recommend reorder quantities based on demand forecasting, so that out-of-stock incidents are minimized.
15. As an Inventory Manager, I want to export replenishment purchase orders to PDF and print barcode labels seamlessly, so that supplier communications and shelf labeling require no manual data re-entry.
16. As an Inventory Manager, I want supplier pullouts for expired or defective goods to track approval statuses and produce manifests, so that supplier credit claims are properly documented.
17. As an Administrator, I want the operational dashboard to display Gross Sales, Net Sales, Gross Profit, and inventory health in compact, real-time metric cards, so that I can evaluate daily store performance at a glance.
18. As an Administrator, I want register management to indicate active terminal connections and assign cash drawers, so that hardware issues on the sales floor are detected early.
19. As an Administrator, I want a store calendar to track cashier shift availability and store blackout dates, so that store scheduling conflicts and coverage gaps are prevented.
20. As an Administrator, I want fiscal periods to be locked after monthly closing, so that backdated modifications to sales or inventory ledgers are prevented.
21. As an Administrator, I want to review, compare, and approve demand forecast machine learning candidate models, so that automated restocking recommendations remain accurate over time.
22. As an Administrator, I want shift reports to break down cash float, cash sales, GCash collections, and refunds, so that daily financial reconciliation is completely auditable.
23. As a Super Administrator, I want a unified user management dashboard with tabs for active staff, dormant accounts, and historical actors, so that store permissions adhere strictly to the principle of least privilege.
24. As a Super Administrator, I want historical actor activity preserved even after staff depart or roles change, so that historical sales receipts and audit trails remain permanently attributable.
25. As a Super Administrator, I want protected audit logs with tamper-evident records and JSON payload inspection, so that any security or financial anomaly can be investigated forensically.
26. As a Super Administrator, I want a platform health center showing system resource usage, queue latency, and database growth, so that system degradation can be addressed proactively.
27. As a Super Administrator, I want encrypted portable database backups with pre-restoration schema validation and an authorized reopening process, so that the store can recover from hardware failure with zero data loss.
28. As a System Auditor, I want automated regression and contract checks to run against isolated fixtures, so that running the audit suite never alters live store operational data.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Audit Slicing Architecture**: Audits, tests, and anomaly remediation will proceed vertically by role workspace (Cashier Workspace -> Inventory Manager Workspace -> Administrator Workspace -> Super Administrator Workspace).
- **Tri-Fold Inspection Seam**: Each view and workflow will be verified across three distinct layers:
  1. Static markup and style bundle audits using the existing project audit scripts.
  2. Service-level PHP contract test execution validating database schema parity, race conditions, and rollback transactions.
  3. Playwright headless browser automation validating real DOM behavior, keyboard shortcuts, modal focus trapping, and layout integrity.
- **Ponytail Rule for Feature Disposition**: When auditing the catalog of views, core promised features (such as batch expiration alerts or register shift reconciliation) will be hardened with automated tests. Incomplete, redundant, or dead abstractions will be retired via documented Architecture Decision Records rather than accumulating speculative maintenance debt.
- **UI/UX Ergonomics and Token System**: UI/UX enhancements will strictly abide by the established design system tokens and density standards. All styles will be bundled through the single CSS bundle generator without introducing external UI framework dependencies.
- **Financial Guardrails**: Implement optimistic double-click prevention on all transactional buttons (e.g., checkout confirmation, refund issuance, fiscal period closure) and enforce distinct confirmation dialogs for destructive actions.
- **Data Table Consistency**: Standardize table density, sticky headers, and non-jumping URL-synchronized pagination across all inventory and reporting views.
- **Non-Destructive Test Execution**: All dynamic tests will run against isolated fixtures or use transactional rollbacks (`RUN_DB_TESTS=1`), ensuring that running the test suite never alters live retail store records.

## Testing Decisions

- **Definition of a Good Test**: A good test asserts external system behavior, state transitions, and business contracts rather than internal implementation trivia. Tests must verify that inputs produce correct domain outputs, ledger balances remain consistent, and unauthorized actions are rejected.
- **Modules and Roles Tested**:
  - Cashier: Point of Sale, GCash portal, Shift management and drawer counts, Cash Refunds and corrections, Stock issue reporting, Transaction history.
  - Inventory Manager: Inventory overview and batch expiration, Product catalog and CSV import, Replenishment queue and PDF generation, Stock receiving, Physical inventory counts, Supplier pullouts.
  - Administrator: Operations dashboard, Register terminal oversight, Store calendar and staff availability, Fiscal period guards, Forecast model review, Financial and shift reporting.
  - Super Administrator: User lifecycle and dormancy policy, Protected audit logs, System health monitoring, Encrypted backup and authorized store reopening.
- **Prior Art and Existing Test Seams**:
  - PHP Contract Tests: `cash_refund_contract.php`, `batch_inventory_ledger_test.php`, `active_workspace_boundaries_contract.php`, `user_lifecycle_contract.php`.
  - Playwright Browser Tests: `cart_workspace_browser_test.js`, `cashier_checkout_receipt_browser_test.js`, `inventory_counts_scan_browser_test.js`, `forecast_decision_browser_test.js`.
  - Static Checkers: `build_styles.php --check`, `audit_views.php`, `smoke_checks.php`.

## Out of Scope

- Multi-store distributed inventory synchronization (RetailMind is strictly a single-store retail operations platform).
- Introduction of third-party heavy component libraries (e.g., Bootstrap, Vuetify, or React) that inflate asset bundle sizes.
- Replacement of the single Random Forest forecasting pipeline with external cloud ML APIs.
- Automatic account merging or general account unification across migrations (all identities remain explicitly reconciled per ADR 0001).

## Further Notes

- The comprehensive view-by-view audit matrix and execution roadmap is preserved in the project artifact directory (`comprehensive_system_audit_and_testing_plan.md`).
- Existing contract tests pass at 113 smoke checks with 0 view markup errors and a verified single CSS bundle. Phase 1 execution will begin with Cashier workspace browser and contract hardening.
title: Comprehensive System Audit, Full Feature Verification, and UI/UX Ergonomics Plan

# Portable Cloudflare Tunnel and Remote Access Toggle

## Problem Statement

The Store owner wants to easily access RetailMind from a smartphone or laptop outside the local store network without performing complicated router port-forwarding or needing a fixed public IP address. At the same time, the owner is not yet ready to purchase a permanent custom domain, but expects whatever solution is built to be seamless to upgrade once a custom domain is acquired. Furthermore, the application will eventually be deployed to a dedicated physical Store PC that is completely separate from the development workstation; setting up the remote access capability on that target PC must be fast, portable, and require minimal technical effort. In addition, the owner desires an intuitive in-app toggle switch within the administrative interface to enable or disable remote access on demand, easily view and copy the active temporary URL, scan a QR code from a mobile device, and monitor connection status from anywhere in the app header.

## Solution

Provide a turnkey, portable Cloudflare Tunnel management solution integrated into RetailMind. The system supports instant temporary public HTTPS connectivity using Cloudflare Quick Tunnels while maintaining a clean architectural path to bind a permanent domain and tunnel token later. Within the Store Configuration settings, an administrator can toggle remote access on or off, inspect current operational status, copy the temporary URL, or scan a generated QR code with a smartphone. A persistent header quick-pill displays live status across all workspaces and provides 1-click URL retrieval. On the deployment side, self-contained, portable Windows scripts allow the entire tunnel daemon to be bootstrapped and installed as an automatic Windows Service on any target PC with zero host machine coupling. Web security guardrails are enforced to shield local databases, configuration secrets, and administrative utilities from untrusted external traffic.

## User Stories

1. As a Store Owner, I want to access my local RetailMind installation from my phone while away from the store, so that I can monitor operations and store activity remotely.
2. As a Store Owner, I want remote access to generate an online HTTPS URL without requiring a custom domain initially, so that I can test remote connectivity immediately without upfront expense.
3. As a Store Owner, I want the system architecture to support an effortless transition to a permanent custom domain in the future, so that I do not need to rewrite or reconfigure application logic when buying a domain.
4. As an Administrator, I want to toggle remote access on or off directly within the Store Configuration view, so that I maintain direct control over when the local application is reachable from the internet.
5. As an Administrator, I want to view the current remote connectivity status (Online vs Offline) in real time, so that I know whether the tunnel daemon is actively serving traffic.
6. As an Administrator, I want to easily copy the active temporary tunnel URL with a single click, so that I can paste it into messaging apps or save it to my phone's browser bookmarks.
7. As an Administrator, I want to view a scannable QR code of the active remote URL, so that I can open the store interface on my mobile phone instantly without manually typing long random URLs.
8. As a Store Owner, I want a persistent status indicator in the top header bar, so that I can verify remote tunnel availability and copy the link from any page without navigating back to settings.
9. As a Deployer, I want portable, self-contained setup scripts that run on any Windows PC, so that deploying RetailMind to a dedicated store machine does not depend on developer workstation paths or manual binary installations.
10. As a Deployer, I want the remote tunnel capable of running as a registered Windows Service, so that remote connectivity automatically resumes after store power outages or PC restarts without manual intervention.
11. As a Store Owner, I want sensitive files like database backups, source control directories, and environment secrets strictly blocked from external requests, so that exposing the local server to the internet does not leak confidential business data.
12. As a Store Owner, I want local Point of Sale checkout and receipt printing to remain fully operational during internet disruptions, so that store sales are never blocked by cloud or connectivity drops.
13. As an Administrator, I want internal assets, stylesheets, scripts, and session cookies to function properly over both local HTTP and remote HTTPS origins, so that remote pages load cleanly without mixed-content errors or broken styles.
14. As an Administrator, I want the option to input a Cloudflare Tunnel Token when a custom domain is acquired, so that the tunnel smoothly binds to our private domain name without needing code refactoring.
15. As a Cashier, I want my physical checkout register and thermal printing to stay isolated on the store counter, so that remote viewers cannot trigger unintended physical till transactions.
16. As a Store Owner, I want remote sessions to obey authentication policies and timeouts, so that leaving a remote browser open does not compromise store governance.
17. As an Administrator, I want stopping the tunnel toggle to immediately sever external access, so that no external connection persists when the store owner wishes to remain strictly local.
18. As a Deployer, I want clear, concise documentation outlining the 5-minute setup process on the target Store PC, so that store personnel or technicians can bring the system online confidently.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Store Configuration Integration**: Add a dedicated Remote Access management card within the Store Configuration settings. This card houses the activation toggle, live status badge, public URL container with a 1-click clipboard copy button, a modal or popover trigger for a mobile-friendly QR code, and a configuration placeholder for future permanent Cloudflare Tunnel tokens.
- **Persistent Header Quick-Pill**: Embed a non-intrusive status pill in the global application header adjacent to notifications. When remote access is active, the pill illuminates green and provides a compact dropdown displaying the active URL and a quick-copy action.
- **Tunnel Orchestration Service**: Implement a backend daemon management abstraction responsible for starting, stopping, inspecting the health of, and extracting the dynamic public URL from the tunnel process. The service maintains process state cleanly and ensures graceful shutdown when disabled.
- **Portability & Host Decoupling**: Isolate all tunnel bootstrap scripts and binary downloads into standalone scripts using relative paths. The scripts automatically detect the target environment, verify local web server responsiveness, fetch the standalone executable if absent, and support both immediate interactive launch and permanent Windows Service installation.
- **Reverse Proxy and Protocol Detection**: Ensure the application's base URL and routing infrastructure dynamically respect reverse proxy headers such as forwarded host and protocol parameters, preventing hardcoded localhost URLs from corrupting remote stylesheets, scripts, and navigation links.
- **Security Boundary & File Lockdown**: Enforce rigorous web server access controls to ensure hidden files, environment definitions, git metadata, internal test fixtures, and raw database backup archives return immediate HTTP 403 Forbidden responses to external requests.
- **Domain Cutover Readiness**: Provide a structured configuration template separating volatile operational parameters (such as credentials and tunnel tokens) from the core application. Upgrading from a temporary quick tunnel to a branded custom domain requires only populating the token within the configuration file, with zero modifications to application source code.

## Testing Decisions

- **Primary Seam: HTTP & Administrative UI End-to-End**:
  - Tests must evaluate externally observable system behavior and user interactions rather than testing raw script strings or private process internals.
  - Test the Store Configuration remote access card to ensure toggling state correctly triggers operational status transitions, updates the live indicator between Offline and Online, and surfaces the retrieved tunnel URL.
  - Test the header status pill to confirm accurate reflection of online state across distinct roles and views.
  - Test the copy button and QR code generator to ensure the output URL accurately matches the current tunnel entrypoint.
- **Security & Route Guardrail Seam**:
  - Execute automated HTTP probes against sensitive locations (environment definitions, version control directories, backup directories) to guarantee access is categorically denied.
  - Verify that mutations restricted to physical store premises (cash drawer balancing, physical register adjustments) respect access policy boundaries when accessed over remote origins.
- **Prior Art**:
  - Leverages existing administrative dashboard route testing, session/authentication policy tests, and store settings persistence test patterns.

## Out of Scope

- Registering or purchasing a custom domain name during the current development iteration.
- Enforcing paid enterprise Cloudflare features or multi-region load balancing.
- Replicating the local transactional database to cloud database instances; local transactions remain authoritative on the physical Store PC.
- Enabling remote cash drawer kicks or triggering remote physical thermal printing.

## Further Notes

This specification addresses the immediate requirement for portable, on-demand remote access with quick-tunnel capabilities while fully honoring the long-term goal of running on a permanent custom domain on a dedicated physical Store PC. Once approved and implemented, transition to a custom domain will require only obtaining the tunnel credentials from the Cloudflare dashboard and entering them into the provided configuration template.
title: Portable Cloudflare Tunnel, Remote Access Toggle, and QR Code

body:
## Context

The two-axis review of PR #436 (issues #430–#434) produced findings that were intentionally deferred because fixing them would change user-visible behaviour, cross a runtime boundary, or need a product decision. The safe, behaviour-preserving findings were fixed in `5f6bb34`. This issue tracks the rest.

## Deferred — would change behaviour (needs a decision)

- **#432 `store_status` routes by reason substring.** `DemandForecastService::getCoverage` still derives `store_status` by string-matching `exclusion_reason` (`'Stale forecast'`, `'Unapproved model'`, `'Insufficient'`) instead of using the module's `exclusion_category`. The coarse categories (`evidence`/`restriction`/`freshness`/`approval`/`recovery`) do not map 1:1 onto the three buckets (`evidence` covers "Forecast unavailable", "Incomplete forecast", and "Insufficient history"), so switching to category alone would misclassify. Decide whether to add a finer category (e.g. `insufficient_history`) or keep the reason check.
- **`ForecastUsability` has two precedence ladders.** `assess()`'s exclusion ladder and `forecastStatus()`'s display ladder order the same conditions differently in edge combinations (approved-empty before vs after superseded; incompatible before vs after superseded; incompatible before vs after model mismatch). Merging them (the reviewer's "derive status from the selected reason") changes the visible status text. Needs a decision on the correct single precedence.

## Deferred — scope judgement

- **#432 Model Review / coverage wiring (user stories 13–14, decisions a1/a2).** `getOperationalIssues` builds narrative issue text from coverage flags (presentation), and `administrator/model_review.php` is an approval surface; neither re-derives the per-Product usability rule, so wiring them to `ForecastUsability` was out of the minimal refactor. Revisit if user stories 13–14 are load-bearing.
- **#432/#434 caller-delegation tests (decision a3/a5).** The named callers are already exercised end-to-end by `replenishment_queue_contract`, `forecast_coverage_contract_test`, `forecast_landing_page_contract_test`, and `demand_forecast_service_test`. Add explicit delegation assertions only if a caller regresses.

## Deferred — accepted, documented

- **`assess()` untyped `$context` array / `forecastStatus()` 13 positional args (Data Clumps).** The array shape is the interface the spec chose; a small value type could replace it, but it is not required for correctness.
- **Cross-language band algorithm duplicated (PHP `ForecastMetrics` + Python `resolve_readiness`).** Only the band data is shared via `forecast_readiness_bands.json`; the algorithm is duplicated and guarded by `forecast_metrics_contract.php`. Accepted for now (two runtimes); revisit if the band logic grows.
- **`ForecastUsability` holds two decisions (buying-usability + readiness ladder).** Deliberate: the spec chose one seam for both so callers do not drift.
title: Forecasting deepening: deferred review follow-ups (PR #436)

body:
## Problem

Running `src/backend/tests/forecasting_runner_installation_test.php` deletes the repository-tracked file `src/backend/config/forecasting_runner.json`.

At the end of the test, `@unlink($configPath)` removes the real config file (`$configPath = $configDir . '/forecasting_runner.json'`), and the test does not restore or recreate the original. The file is tracked by git, so after a test run the working tree shows an unintended deletion.

## Impact

- Leaves the local working tree dirty after running tests.
- `StoreModelGovernanceService`, `src/backend/scripts/run_scheduler.php`, and the model-review component read this file to resolve the models directory; while they degrade gracefully when it is absent, the tracked configuration is silently lost until restored.
- Any agent/CI that runs the test then commits would capture the deletion.

## Expected

The test should not mutate a tracked repository file. It should either operate on a temporary config directory, or snapshot and restore the original file (including creating it if it did not exist) in a `finally` block.

## Evidence

- `src/backend/tests/forecasting_runner_installation_test.php` L38 (`$configPath = $configDir . '/forecasting_runner.json'`) and L269 (`@unlink($configPath)`).

Discovered while running the forecasting test suite during the #430–#434 deepening work.
title: fix(tests): forecasting_runner_installation_test deletes the tracked forecasting_runner.json

body:
## Problem Statement

The "complete 28-day Forecast Horizon" aggregate — summing a Product's daily Demand Forecast values into 7-, 14-, and 28-day totals with a completeness check — is written out five times: in Demand Forecast reads, the Replenishment Queue, Store Reports generation, and the dashboard. Tests currently scrape the SQL out of production source with a regular expression to exercise it, so the tests break on any formatting change and can pass while production drifts. A change to the completeness rule has to be applied in five places.

## Solution

Introduce `ForecastAggregateReader`, a deep module with one small interface that returns, per Product for a job, the 7/14/28-day sums plus Forecast Origin, model version, readiness level, limitation marker, and a completeness flag. All five callers ask the module instead of embedding their own aggregate query.

## User Stories

1. As an Inventory Manager, I want the 7/14/28-day totals computed identically everywhere, so that purchase quantities agree between the Replenishment Queue and Store Reports.
2. As an Administrator, I want an incomplete Demand Forecast rejected consistently, so that no surface shows partial totals.
3. As a Super Administrator, I want completeness defined once, so that a Product cannot be complete on one page and incomplete on another.
4. As a developer, I want to change the aggregate rule once, so that all callers follow.
5. As a developer, I want to test the aggregate directly, so that I no longer scrape SQL out of source.
6. As a developer, I want the aggregate to expose Forecast Origin, model version, readiness level, and limitation marker, so that callers do not each re-select them.
7. As an Inventory Manager, I want the Replenishment Recommendation's expected sales to come from the shared aggregate, so that the number matches the forecast page.
8. As an Administrator, I want dashboard forecast figures to match the forecasting workspace, so that oversight is trustworthy.
9. As a developer, I want Store Reports generation to consume the reader, so that report totals cannot drift from the Replenishment Queue.
10. As a developer, I want one place that knows the schema-probe fallbacks for optional columns, so that callers do not each probe.
11. As a Super Administrator, I want only successful Forecast Generation jobs to yield aggregates, so that failed or observation runs never leak into totals.
12. As a developer, I want the reader to return typed integers, so that view arithmetic needs no casting.
13. As an Inventory Manager, I want per-Product totals keyed by Product id, so that lookups are direct.
14. As a developer, I want a single query builder for the 7/14/28 CASE sums, so that performance tuning happens once.
15. As a developer, I want the reader to support both a specific job and the latest usable job, so that callers do not re-implement job selection.
16. As an operator, I want no visible change to totals, so that the consolidation is invisible.

## Implementation Decisions

- New module `ForecastAggregateReader` with one interface returning per-Product aggregates for a given job, or for the latest usable job.
- Aggregate includes: 7/14/28-day sums, Forecast Origin, model version, readiness level, limitation marker, and a completeness flag.
- The completeness rule (28 rows, distinct horizon days 1 through 28, a single Forecast Origin and model version, non-negative prediction) lives only in this module.
- Schema-probe fallbacks for optional columns move into the reader.
- Callers — Demand Forecast reads, Replenishment Queue build, Store Reports generation, dashboard — stop embedding their own `SUM(CASE ...)` block.
- The regex source-scraping test is replaced by a direct reader test.
- Depends on nothing else; unblocks the forecast-usability spec.
- ADR-0005 fixes the 7-, 14-, and 28-day Forecast Horizons; this module implements that fixed shape.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test asserts external behaviour: for a given database state, the reader returns the expected per-Product totals and completeness. No assertions about the generated SQL string.
- Cover: complete forecast, incomplete (missing a horizon day), multiple Forecast Origins in one job, multiple model versions, negative predictions, and a failed job (no aggregates).
- Assert each caller delegates rather than recomputes.
- Prior art: `src/backend/tests/demand_forecast_service_test.php` (which currently does the regex scraping) and `replenishment_queue_contract.php`.
- Seam: one new seam, `ForecastAggregateReader`.

## Out of Scope

- Migrating stored forecast data.
- Changing any total's value or rounding.
- Performance work beyond removing the duplication.

## Further Notes

- Honours ADR-0005.
- This is the natural first step of the forecasting deepening set; the usability module consumes it.
title: Collapse the complete 28-day forecast aggregate into one module
